stories.headline: Eisenkot gets the mandate: can he reach 61 seats?
stories.question: Can Gadi Eisenkot actually build a coalition that ends the Netanyahu era in Israel?
stories.dek: On 7 November, Herzog chose Eisenkot to form Israel's next government. Eisenkot's alliance has 48 of 120 seats and needs 61. Two ultra-Orthodox parties could close the gap, or outside support could keep a minority government in office.

so_far.text: Israel voted on 27 October 2026. Its parliament, the Knesset, has 120 seats, so a government needs 61. Eisenkot's four-party alliance won 48 seats, Netanyahu's bloc won 53, and Arab-led parties won a record 19. According to AP, Likud was the biggest single party with 27 seats, six more than Eisenkot's Yashar party. Party leaders then told President Isaac Herzog whom they backed. In all, 67 lawmakers, including some from Arab-led parties, recommended Eisenkot. Only 46 backed Netanyahu.

what_happened.text: On 7 November 2026, President Herzog chose opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief, over Netanyahu to form the next government. The mandate, meaning the formal task of building that government, was due to be formalised on Sunday, 8 November. Eisenkot gets 28 days, and this can be extended by 14. He has ruled out a government that includes Arab-led parties. He also says he will not serve in a Netanyahu government, even in a rotation deal, where two leaders take turns as prime minister. His reason is Netanyahu's responsibility for 7 October. Sources close to Netanyahu have suggested a unity government.

steps.text: A government needs a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, which means 61 seats.
Eisenkot's alliance has 48 seats, so he needs 13 more from parties outside it.
Shas and UTJ, two ultra-Orthodox parties, would bring him to exactly 61. Their conditions are not yet known.
Without them, he could form a minority government. He would need to win a confidence vote, with Arab-led parties supporting him from outside.
If he fails, other candidates get a turn. After that comes a new election within 90 days, with Netanyahu as caretaker.

lesson.concept: How a government is formed in Israel's Knesset
lesson.big_idea: A government needs the backing of the 120-seat Knesset. The simplest route is a coalition with 61 seats. A smaller minority government can also take office if enough outsiders vote for it.

steps.title: Count to 61
steps.text: Israel's parliament, the Knesset, has 120 seats. A majority is half plus one, which is 61. An alliance holding 61 seats can win votes on its own and keep its government in office.

steps.title: The president picks who tries
steps.text: After an election, party leaders tell the president whom they recommend. The president then gives the mandate, the task of forming a government, to one candidate. Eisenkot has 28 days, plus up to 14 more.

steps.title: Coalition: add partners' seats
steps.text: Few parties win 61 seats alone. So the mandate-holder offers partners ministries and policy promises, and their seats are added together. Eisenkot's alliance has 48 seats. Shas and UTJ would take him to exactly 61.

steps.title: Minority government: win the vote
steps.text: A government with fewer than 61 seats can still take office by winning a confidence vote, meaning a Knesset vote that approves it. Parties outside the government can vote yes without getting any ministries.

steps.title: If nobody succeeds
steps.text: If the first nominee fails, the president picks another. If that also fails, a Knesset majority can back a third person, who gets 14 days. After that comes a new election within 90 days, with Netanyahu as caretaker.

example.setup: Imagine a 120-seat parliament. Asha leads an alliance with 50 seats. Her rivals hold 50. The other 20 seats belong to parties she won't take into government.

lines.label: Majority line
lines.note: Half the seats plus one.

lines.label: Route A: coalition
lines.note: Partners join the government, so Asha has a majority of her own.

lines.label: Route B: outsiders abstain
lines.note: Assume a confidence vote needs more yes votes than no votes. A tie fails.

lines.label: Route B: outsiders vote yes
lines.note: She passes, but the 20 hold no ministries and can withdraw support later.

example.result: A coalition gives Asha 61 seats of her own. A minority government can also work. But when her rivals have as many seats as she does, the outsiders must actually vote yes. Abstaining is not enough.

apply.text: Eisenkot is in Asha's position, with harder numbers. His alliance has 48 seats and Netanyahu's bloc has 53. Route A means winning over Shas and UTJ to reach exactly 61. Route B means a minority government. Ahmad Tibi expects Arab-led parties to support that from outside. Netanyahu calls such a government dangerous. Eisenkot has ruled out Arab-led parties inside his government.

practice.q: Use the real numbers: Eisenkot 48 seats, Netanyahu's bloc 53, Arab-led parties 19. Assume all 53 vote no. Does Eisenkot pass if the 19 abstain? What if they vote yes?
practice.answer: If they abstain: 48 yes vs 53 no, so he fails. If they vote yes: 48 + 19 = 67 yes vs 53 no, so he passes. With these numbers, outside support must mean actual yes votes, not just abstentions.

check.why: Recommendations only decide who tries first. A government with fewer than 61 seats can still take office if the Knesset approves it in a confidence vote.

stories.question: Is Trump escalating or winding down the Iran war after losing Congress?
stories.dek: Both at once. On 6 November US forces hit Iranian air defences on Qeshm Island, and the US is looking to widen its blockade. Yet Trump says Iran wants a deal.

so_far.text: The United States and Iran are at war. US forces run a naval blockade, stopping ships that trade with Iran. Iran says tankers have hit mines near the Strait of Hormuz. Nobody has confirmed these claims, and Trump says Iran makes them up to raise energy prices. Qatar is mediating indirect talks between the two sides. In May 2026 the Senate voted 50-47 to limit the war, but a veto was seen as likely. On 3 November Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections. Trump blamed the loss partly on the Iran war.

what_happened.text: On Friday 6 November US forces carried out what Trump called 'minor strikes' on Iranian air-defence systems on Qeshm Island. These were the first US strikes since the 3 November midterms. Iranian state media reported two missile strikes in the Suza area of the island. Iran's army said it shot down a US MQ-9 drone. Trump then spoke with Qatar's emir and said a decision on new strikes would come soon. He also said Iran 'wants to make a deal'. On 7 November Reuters reported that the US military is looking to widen its blockade to Iran's trade by land. CENTCOM has set up a team for this, called Task Force Iron Gate.

steps.text: Democrats won Congress on 3 November, but they take control only in January. That leaves Trump about two months.
Vance called the war 'the reason we lost', and Trump admitted high fuel prices hurt Republicans. That is a reason to seek a deal.
But Asia Times analysts warn a cornered president may escalate instead, while his room to act lasts.
So the US mixes pressure and talks: small strikes, a wider blockade, a reward for nuclear tips, and calls with Qatar.
Congress's brakes are weak: a president can veto a war vote, so investigations and spending limits are its main tools.

lesson.concept: How Congress can and cannot stop a war
lesson.big_idea: A president runs the military, but Congress can vote to end a war. A simple majority passes that vote, but if the president vetoes it, two-thirds are needed to win.

steps.title: Two branches share war
steps.text: The president commands the military and can order strikes. Congress declares war and controls the money. Neither can fully run a war alone, so each has ways to push the other.

steps.title: A vote to stop the war
steps.text: Congress can pass a war powers resolution, an order telling the president to end military action. A simple majority in each house is enough. In May 2026 the Senate passed one on Iran, 50-47.

steps.title: The veto and two-thirds
steps.text: The president can veto, or reject, that resolution. Congress can override the veto only with two-thirds of both houses. In the Senate that means 67 votes.

steps.title: The old Congress stays until January
steps.text: Election winners do not take over at once. Democrats won on 3 November but take control in January. That leaves Trump about two months with the old Congress.

steps.title: Money and questions
steps.text: If votes fall short, Congress can still limit spending on the war or hold investigations. Experts doubt these tools can stop escalation.

example.setup: Suppose the new Senate votes 55 to 45 to end the war, and all 100 senators vote. Assume the House has passed the same resolution.

lines.label: Majority needed
lines.note: A simple majority passes the resolution.

lines.label: Does it pass?
lines.note: It now goes to the president.

lines.label: President vetoes
lines.note: A veto cancels it unless Congress overrides.

lines.label: Override needed
lines.note: Same rule applies in the House too.

lines.label: The shortfall
lines.note: The veto stands; the war goes on.

example.result: A clear majority can pass a vote to end a war and still lose to a veto. To win, 12 senators who voted no would have to switch sides.

apply.text: This is why the May Senate vote of 50-47 was not expected to survive a veto: it was 17 short of 67. Democrats take control only in January, giving Trump about two months. Even then, experts doubt Congress can stop escalation and expect it to use investigations and spending limits instead.

practice.q: Say the Senate votes 60 to 40 to end the war, with all 100 voting, and the president vetoes. How many more yes votes are needed?
practice.answer: 60 is more than 50, so it passes. The veto blocks it. Override needs two-thirds of 100, which is 67. 67 − 60 = 7. Seven senators who voted no must switch, and the House also needs two-thirds.

stories.question: Is the petrol at Indian pumps carrying far more ethanol than the 20% limit?
stories.dek: Karnataka's tests found up to 31.2% ethanol in some petrol samples. Three big oil companies say their 893 tests show 19–21%. The answer affects mileage across India's 35 crore vehicles.

so_far.text: Indian oil companies sell E20 petrol: petrol blended with ethanol, an alcohol fuel, with a 20% limit. They say it meets the Bureau of Indian Standards specification IS 17021. Karnataka's minister says vehicles made after April 2023 are certified only for E20. Some motorists have complained of lower mileage and frequent repairs. In October 2026, Union Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri called concerns about E20 a 'contrived narrative'. He said there were no plans to go beyond 20%. In the same month, Karnataka collected petrol samples to test.

what_happened.text: On 6 November 2026, Karnataka's Food and Civil Supplies Minister Rizwan Arshad announced results from 63 petrol samples taken in seven districts. Many were above the 20% ethanol limit. The highest was 31.2% in an IOCL sample, then 30.5% in an HPCL Power sample. The lowest was 13.5%. ThePrint reports that Shriram Research Institute, a Bengaluru lab, did the tests. After the announcement, IOCL, BPCL and HPCL jointly rejected the findings. They said Karnataka skipped the prescribed procedure. They said their own 893 samples from 27 states and union territories were all within 19–21% ethanol.

steps.text: E20 means one litre in five is ethanol, and ethanol holds less energy per litre than petrol.
So more ethanol in each litre means less energy, and a vehicle travels fewer kilometres per litre.
Karnataka's minister says vehicles made after April 2023 are certified only for E20, so higher blends fall outside that.
Karnataka says a lab found up to 31.2%; the oil companies say only tests under the prescribed procedure count.
So the fight is less about chemistry and more about whose sampling and testing can be trusted.

lesson.concept: What E20 means and why the ethanol share matters
lesson.big_idea: E20 petrol is one-fifth ethanol. Ethanol holds less energy than petrol, so more ethanol means fewer kilometres per litre. That is why the exact percentage, and how it is tested, matters.

steps.title: E20 means one-fifth ethanol
steps.text: E20 is petrol with ethanol, an alcohol fuel, mixed in. The 20 means 20% of the volume is ethanol, so one litre in five. The oil companies say their E20 meets the Bureau of Indian Standards specification IS 17021.

steps.title: Ethanol carries less energy
steps.text: A litre of ethanol releases less energy when burned than a litre of petrol. So the more ethanol each litre holds, the less energy it carries, and the fewer kilometres it moves you.

steps.title: The ministry's mileage estimate
steps.text: A Petroleum Ministry assessment from August 2025, cited by the oil companies, says vehicles designed for E20 may lose 1–2% mileage. Other vehicles may lose 3–6%. So engines built for the blend lose less.

steps.title: Certified blend, and fair testing
steps.text: Karnataka's minister says vehicles made after April 2023 are certified only for E20. To prove a pump went over, the oil companies say six one-litre samples are needed: two for the dealer, two kept back, two for an authorised lab.

example.setup: Say you fill 10 litres of petrol. Assume a litre of ethanol holds two-thirds the energy of a litre of petrol. Compare a correct E20 fill with a 30% fill.

lines.label: E20 tank
lines.calc: 20% of 10 L = 2 L ethanol, 8 L petrol
lines.note: One litre in five is ethanol.

lines.label: E20 energy
lines.note: Counted as litres of pure petrol, using our assumption.

lines.label: 30% tank
lines.calc: 30% of 10 L = 3 L ethanol, 7 L petrol
lines.note: One more litre of ethanol, one less of petrol.

lines.label: 30% energy
lines.note: Same assumption as before.

lines.label: The gap
lines.note: Compared with a correct E20 tank.

example.result: Ten extra points of ethanol cut the energy in your tank by roughly 3.6%. This is a rough guide; the real change in mileage depends on the engine and how it is tuned.

apply.text: Karnataka's highest reading, 31.2%, is close to the 30% tank in our example: nearly a third ethanol instead of a fifth. The oil companies' 893 samples at 19–21% match the E20 tank. Both cannot describe the same fuel. So the fight now turns on step four: whether Karnataka's sampling followed the prescribed procedure.

practice.q: Same 10 litres, but the petrol is 25% ethanol. Using the same two-thirds assumption, how much energy do you lose compared with correct E20?
practice.answer: Ethanol: 25% of 10 = 2.5 litres, so petrol is 7.5 litres. Energy: 7.5 + (2.5 × ⅔) ≈ 7.5 + 1.67 = 9.17 litres' worth. E20 gave 9.33. Gap: 9.33 − 9.17 ≈ 0.17. Then 0.17 ÷ 9.33 ≈ 1.8% less energy.

stories.headline: Delhi-NCR moves to GRAP Stage III as Diwali smog thickens
stories.question: What does GRAP Stage III change for Delhi-NCR residents this Diwali?
stories.dek: Stage III halts non-essential construction, bans older petrol and diesel cars in Delhi and nearby cities, limits interstate buses and puts young children on hybrid classes. Smoke from farm fires stays outside its reach.

so_far.text: GRAP, the Graded Response Action Plan, is Delhi-NCR's step-by-step list of anti-pollution curbs. The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) decides when each stage starts. Calm winds and a temperature inversion trap pollutants near the ground. An inversion is a warm layer of air that sits on top like a lid. Independent studies blame stubble fires in Punjab and Haryana for up to 45% of Delhi's PM2.5 (tiny airborne particles) in peak season. After Diwali 2025, IQAir recorded 1,121 on private monitors. Only 11 of 39 official stations reported data on Diwali night.

what_happened.text: On 6 November 2026, CAQM invoked GRAP Stage III across Delhi-NCR with immediate effect. It acted at an AQI of 382, before the 400 'severe' line was crossed. Stage III halts non-essential construction across NCR, including drilling, piling and excavation. It bans BS-III petrol and BS-IV diesel four-wheelers in Delhi and nearby cities. It also restricts interstate buses and brings hybrid classes for Classes 1–5. At 8 am on 7 November, Diwali eve, Delhi's AQI was 364 ('very poor'). Several stations were in the severe range. IQAir ranked Delhi the world's most polluted major city that day.

steps.text: Calm winds and a temperature inversion trap smoke and dust near the ground, so pollution builds up instead of blowing away.
CAQM invoked Stage III pre-emptively on 6 November, at AQI 382, before the 400 'severe' line was crossed.
Stage III cuts local sources inside NCR: construction dust, exhaust from older vehicles, and interstate buses.
It cannot touch stubble fires in Punjab and Haryana, which studies link to up to 45% of peak-season PM2.5.
IITM's early warning system still expects 'severe' air from 7 to 9 November; IMD sees mostly clear skies and no warnings.

lesson.concept: How GRAP tightens curbs as the AQI climbs
lesson.big_idea: GRAP links Delhi-NCR's air quality number to a ladder of rules. As the air gets worse, CAQM moves up a stage, and each stage adds stricter curbs.

steps.title: AQI turns air into one number
steps.text: The AQI combines readings of pollutants, such as PM2.5, into one score. Higher means dirtier air. Delhi's 364 on 7 November counted as 'very poor'. Above 400 counts as 'severe'.

steps.title: GRAP ties the number to rules
steps.text: CAQM runs GRAP. As the air gets worse, it moves Delhi-NCR up a stage. Each stage adds stricter curbs on top of the ones before.

steps.title: Stage III targets local sources
steps.text: Stage III halts non-essential construction, including drilling, piling and excavation. It bans BS-III petrol and BS-IV diesel four-wheelers in Delhi and nearby cities. It restricts interstate buses and brings hybrid classes for Classes 1–5.

steps.title: Stage III came before 400
steps.text: CAQM invoked Stage III on 6 November at AQI 382, before the 400 'severe' line was crossed. Reports call the move pre-emptive. No source gives CAQM's reasoning.

steps.title: The next line is 450
steps.text: Stage IV is being watched if the AQI goes above 450. It may include odd-even rationing, where cars run on alternate days by number plate.

apply.text: Delhi is the real case. CAQM moved at 382 on 6 November, just under the severe line. Reports call it pre-emptive but give no reason. At 8 am on 7 November the AQI was 364, below 400, and Stage IV is watched only above 450. But Stage III cuts only NCR's own dust and exhaust. Stubble smoke from Punjab and Haryana is outside its reach.

practice.q: Say a city's AQI reads 372 on Saturday morning. How far is it from the 400 'severe' line and the 450 Stage IV line?
practice.answer: Severe line: 400 − 372 = 28 points. Stage IV line: 450 − 372 = 78 points. So the air is below severe, and much further from the level where Stage IV is watched.

stories.headline: What Democrats plan for AI, and why tech stocks fell
stories.question: What AI rules are Democrats planning, and why did tech shares lose $2 trillion?
stories.dek: Democrats plan bills on AI testing, company liability and data-centre power costs. Investors fear slower AI building, so they paid less for chip shares before any law existed.

so_far.text: In the 2026 US midterm elections, Democrats made gains in Congress. AI and chip shares fell hard after the result. Investors fear Democrats will slow the building of data centres, the giant computer halls that run AI. The fight had been building for months. In March 2026, Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez proposed a pause on new AI data centres. In September 2026, Senate Democrats blocked a Republican data-centre cost bill because it was voluntary. In the election, data centres appeared on 41 ballot measures in 10 states.

what_happened.text: On 7 November, a Reuters report, carried in an aggregator summary, said Democrats are preparing AI bills for when they take control of Congress in January. The bills would cover data-centre electricity costs, independent testing of advanced AI, and company liability for harm. Rep. Lori Trahan is reportedly drafting the testing and liability bill. Sen. Martin Heinrich's GRID Savings Act would stop grid costs being passed to communities. Donald Trump blamed Democrats for the crash, and the White House postponed a tech advisory council meeting. On 6 November the Nasdaq rose 1.09%, but stayed well below its level before the fall.

steps.text: AI companies need data centres, and chip makers like Nvidia, Micron and AMD sell their chips into them.
Voters backed data-centre restrictions in all but one of 41 ballot measures, showing appetite for limits.
Democratic bills on power costs, testing and liability could make data centres costlier and slower to build.
Slower building means fewer chip orders, so investors cut their guesses of chip makers' future profits.

lesson.concept: How fear of future rules moves share prices
lesson.big_idea: A share price is what investors will pay for a company's future profits. If new rules might shrink those profits, the price falls straight away, long before any law passes.

steps.title: A share buys future profits
steps.text: When you buy a share, you buy a small slice of a company's future profits. So the price reflects what investors expect those profits to be.

steps.title: Price is profit times a multiple
steps.text: A simple way investors price a share: expected yearly profit per share, times a number called the multiple. A high multiple means investors feel confident and expect growth.

steps.title: Expected profit can change overnight
steps.text: Chip makers sell to AI data centres. If voters and lawmakers might slow data-centre building, investors expect fewer chip orders and lower profits, even with no law yet.

steps.title: Uncertainty lowers the multiple too
steps.text: When the rules are unclear, investors also pay less for each rupee of profit. So the price can fall by more than the cut in expected profit.

steps.title: Prices can bounce back
steps.text: If the fear eases, investors raise their guesses again. The Nasdaq fell 5.5% on 5 November, then rose 1.09% on 6 November.

example.setup: Say a chip company is expected to earn ₹10 per share a year, and investors pay 30 times that profit (assume this multiple).

lines.label: Price before the news
lines.note: Expected profit times the multiple.

lines.label: Profit guess cut 10%
lines.note: Fewer data centres may mean fewer chip orders.

lines.label: Multiple cut
lines.note: Unclear rules make investors pay less per rupee of profit.

lines.label: New price
lines.note: Both changes together.

lines.label: Total fall
lines.note: Bigger than the 10% cut in profit.

example.result: A 10% cut in expected profit, plus a little extra caution, knocked 19% off the price. That is how a fear, not a law, can wipe out huge sums in one day.

apply.text: On 5 November, investors feared Democrats might raise data-centre costs and add testing and liability rules. Like our made-up company, real chip makers fell sharply: Micron 17%, AMD more than 17%, Nvidia about 9%. On 6 November they partly recovered: Nvidia about 3%, Micron 5%, AMD about 11%. Separately, analysts quoted on 4 November doubted any law could meaningfully halt data-centre building.

practice.q: Same company, now at ₹243. Suppose the fear fades: expected profit returns to ₹10, but the multiple stays at 27. What is the new price?
practice.answer: New price = ₹10 × 27 = ₹270. That is ₹27 above ₹243, about an 11% rise. But it is still ₹30, or 10%, below the ₹300 before the scare, because caution remains.

Fear of Democratic AI and data-centre rules wiped a reported $2 trillion off US tech shares.

sections.title: World
sections.gist: Paraguay's ousted president is charged over a bank collapse. New Zealand's election is too close to call. Shootings in Kraków and airstrikes in Yemen kill dozens.

items.headline: New Zealand election too close to call, with National largest party
items.text: On 7 November, with over 95% of votes counted, New Zealand's election was still too close to call. Fewer than 4,000 votes separated the two main parties. The Guardian reports that National will be the largest party in parliament. The New York Times says the right-wing bloc was slightly ahead, but no side had a clear win. Voters turned to minor parties in an election dominated by worries about the economy. Official results are expected later in November, once special votes are counted. The Guardian says it may take weeks to know the shape of the next government.
items.background: To govern, a party needs a majority of seats in parliament. If no party has one, it must win support from smaller parties.
items.why: There is no direct effect on India. It shows how small parties can decide who governs when big parties are nearly tied.

items.headline: Paraguay's impeached president Peña under house arrest, then charged
items.text: Paraguay's Congress impeached President Santiago Peña, and he was placed under house arrest minutes later, the Guardian reported on 7 November. Later on 7 November, Al Jazeera and the BBC reported that he had been charged. The case comes from the collapse of Ueno Bank. The Guardian says the banking crisis has left 60% of the country unable to reach their bank accounts. That is more than half of all people. Protesters took to the streets demanding answers. The exact charges are not yet clear. It is also not yet known when people will get access to their money.
items.background: Paraguay's central bank seized Ueno Bank, a digital lender with about 3 million customers, after finding insider loans and expenses recorded as assets.
items.why: It shows how one bank's failure can freeze a country's payments and bring down a government. No direct effect on India.

items.headline: Saudi airstrikes near Yemen's capital kill 27, Houthis say
items.text: On 7 November, Saudi airstrikes hit homes in al-Shariya, near Yemen's capital Sanaa. The Houthi health ministry says 27 people were killed and 36 wounded, mostly women and children. AP also reports at least 27 dead and 36 wounded. An earlier toll from a Houthi official, reported by the Washington Post, was 25 dead, so the count rose during the day. Saudi Arabia has not commented. No one has independently checked the numbers. It is not yet known what the strikes were aimed at.
items.background: The Houthis are an armed group in Yemen that runs its own government ministries. The death toll comes from their health ministry.
items.why: Most of the dead were women and children, according to the Houthi count. No independent figures exist yet.

items.headline: Gunman kills six in Kraków's Main Market Square
items.text: On 7 November a gunman killed six people, four women and two men, in Kraków's Main Market Square in Poland. More than a dozen others were injured. Prime Minister Donald Tusk went to the city. Tusk said three people believed to be the gunman's relatives were found dead at his home. That would bring the number of dead to nine. Poland's interior minister said the attacker appeared "fascinated by far-right ideologies". Investigators have not yet confirmed a motive. Reports so far have not said what happened to the gunman.
items.background: Kraków is one of Poland's largest cities. The Main Market Square is its central public square.
items.why: The interior minister's remark points to a possible far-right motive. Investigators have not yet confirmed it.

items.headline: Trump's new chief of staff once accused India of funding Russia's war
items.text: On 6 November President Trump named Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff. Miller replaces Susie Wiles. The change came days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections. NDTV reported on 7 November that Miller has criticised India before over Russian oil and trade. In August 2025, as deputy chief of staff, Miller said India's purchases of Russian oil were effectively funding the war in Ukraine. He also said India was nearly tied with China as a buyer of that oil. It is not yet known whether his views will change US policy towards India.
items.background: The White House chief of staff runs the president's office and controls who gets the president's time and attention.
items.why: Someone who has called India's Russian oil purchases war funding now has the US president's closest working job.

sections.title: India
sections.gist: The IAF sets a landing record near the China border. The EC reopens voter lists in seven states. Abhishek Banerjee alleges an attack on his home.

items.headline: IAF sets landing record at Nyoma; Army calls Arunachal incursion claims fake
items.text: Mint reported on 7 November that an Indian Air Force IL-76MD transport plane landed at Nyoma airbase in eastern Ladakh. The airbase sits at 13,629 ft. That is a world record for the highest landing by an aircraft of its class. Nyoma is about 25 km from the China border. Mint says the landing strengthens India's ability to fly troops and supplies to the area. Separately, on 7 November the Indian Army and MeitY, the IT ministry, called reports of a 50-km Chinese incursion into Arunachal Pradesh fake. They said six Pakistan-sponsored social media accounts spread those reports within 11 hours.
items.background: India and China share a long, disputed border. Ladakh in the west and Arunachal Pradesh in the east are both along it.
items.why: Big transport planes landing so close to the border can move troops faster. Fake incursion claims can stoke public alarm.

items.headline: EC gives voters dropped from draft rolls in seven states another chance
items.text: On 6 November the Election Commission (EC) told seven states, including Delhi and Maharashtra, to give left-out voters a fresh chance. These are voters missing from the draft rolls of SIR, the EC's special revision of voter lists. They can now apply to be included in the final rolls. The voters had been marked as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate, because they did not return their enumeration forms. Separately, on 7 November The Reporters' Collective reported that nearly 2 lakh voters the EC had declared dead were confirmed alive for panchayat (village council) elections. The deadlines for applying have not been reported.
items.background: SIR is the EC's door-to-door check of voter lists. Opposition parties have protested against it, saying genuine voters could lose their vote.
items.why: If you are missing from your state's draft voter list, this may be your chance to get back on.

items.headline: Abhishek Banerjee alleges attack on his Kolkata home, blames BJP supporters
items.text: Abhishek Banerjee said his home in Kolkata was attacked, and he blamed BJP supporters. He called it the seventh attempt on his life in six months, The Hindu reported on 7 November. News18 reports that he said the attack happened during his birthday celebrations. Banerjee later said the siege lasted much longer than first reported. Mamata Banerjee and the BJP traded charges over the incident. Reports so far do not set out the BJP's full response. It is not yet known whether police have identified or arrested anyone.
items.background: Mamata Banerjee and the BJP are political rivals in West Bengal. Mamata has backed Abhishek Banerjee's account.
items.why: An alleged attack on a senior politician's home raises tension between West Bengal's main political rivals.

items.headline: IndiGo Bengaluru–Lucknow flight turns back after hijack threat note
items.text: On 7 November IndiGo flight 6E-451 left Terminal 1 of Bengaluru's Kempegowda International Airport for Lucknow. After take-off, cabin crew found a note in a toilet. It read: "This flight is going to hijack at 6.30, ignore and see the consequences". Following safety rules, the pilots turned the plane around and flew back to Bengaluru. A full emergency was declared at the airport so security checks could be carried out. It is not yet known who wrote the note. There are no reports of anyone being arrested.
items.background: Airlines treat every written threat as real until security checks prove otherwise. That is why planes turn back even when a threat may be a hoax.
items.why: Threat notes like this force planes to turn back, delaying every passenger on board while security checks the aircraft.

sections.title: Your money & life
sections.gist: Prices of 543 anti-cancer medicine brands fall from 9 November, and the RBI says viral claims of new January 2027 cheque rules are fake.

items.headline: RBI says viral 'new cheque rules from January 2027' are fake
items.text: Posts on social media claim that new cheque book rules start in January 2027. The RBI, India's central bank, says those claims are fake. NDTV and India.com reported its denial on 7 November 2026. The posts refer to CTS, the Cheque Truncation System. Under CTS, banks clear a cheque by sending a scanned image of it rather than moving the paper between branches. The RBI asked people to rely only on information that it publishes. So if a forwarded message announces a new banking rule, check whether the RBI itself has said it before you act.
items.background: The RBI regulates how banks clear cheques. Any real change to cheque rules would come from its own notices.
items.why: These posts need no action from you. Forwarded 'RBI rules' can be false, so check the RBI's own notices.

sections.title: Markets & money
sections.gist: Coca-Cola's India bottler files for an IPO, Brent has its biggest weekly fall since the pandemic, and the RBI tightens rules on gold-backed farm loans.

items.headline: Coca-Cola's India bottler files for IPO, but receives none of the money
items.text: Hindustan Coca-Cola Holdings (HCCH), Coca-Cola's bottling company in India, has filed draft papers for an initial public offering (IPO). An IPO is a company's first sale of shares to the public. Business Standard and Mint reported the filing on 7 November 2026. The whole IPO is an 'offer for sale'. That means an existing owner sells shares it already holds, and no new shares are created. Here the seller is the majority owner, Hindustan Coca-Cola Overseas Holdings, which will sell up to 15% of HCCH. All the money goes to that seller, not to HCCH. HCCH reported ₹11,663 crore in revenue in FY26, about ₹32 crore a day. The reports do not say why the owner is selling now. The price and dates are not yet set.
items.background: A draft prospectus is the first formal step towards an IPO. Regulators must review it before a sale date and price are set.
items.why: Once the IPO opens, Indian investors could buy a part of Coca-Cola's India bottling business.

items.headline: Brent oil has its biggest weekly fall since the pandemic
items.text: Brent crude is a benchmark oil price. In the week ending 6 November 2026, it had its biggest weekly fall since the pandemic. Traders had built a 'war premium' into the price. A war premium is the extra amount buyers pay because they fear a war could cut supply. That premium began to unwind, so prices fell. The weekly fall came even though Brent jumped on 6 November, after an attack on Iran's South Pars gas field. The reports give no price levels. Watch whether the fall holds, or whether new attacks push the premium back up.
items.background: Many oil deals around the world are priced off Brent. When Brent moves, what countries pay for crude oil moves with it.
items.why: India buys much of its oil from abroad. A lower Brent price can reduce its import bill, if the fall lasts.

items.headline: US presses China to honour Busan trade deal on rare earths
items.text: On 6 November 2026, US Treasury Secretary Bessent and Trade Representative Greer pressed China's Vice Premier He Lifeng. They urged China to keep the promises it made in the Busan trade deal. Their concerns were rare earths, other critical minerals and Chinese purchases of US farm goods. Rare earths are metals used to make strong magnets for things like electric cars and phones. According to Mint, the US said China must honour the deal 'fully and immediately'. The Financial Times also reported the warning. Business Times said it came ahead of meetings between Trump and Xi. The reports do not give dates for those meetings.
items.background: In the Busan deal, the US and China agreed to trade terms. The US now says China must deliver its side immediately.
items.why: There is no direct effect on India yet. But rare earth supply matters to electronics and car makers worldwide.

items.headline: RBI tightens rules for counting gold-backed farm loans
items.text: The RBI has tightened the rules on when a farm loan backed by gold counts as priority sector lending (PSL). The Times of India reported the change on 7 November 2026. Here is how PSL works. The RBI requires banks to lend a set share of their money to sectors it wants to support, such as farming. Only loans that qualify count towards that target. In a gold-backed farm loan, a farmer pledges gold to borrow. Tighter rules mean fewer of these loans can be counted. The report does not give the new conditions. It is not yet known how much this will change lending by banks or gold-loan companies.
items.background: Under RBI rules, banks must direct a share of their loans to 'priority sectors' such as agriculture.
items.why: It changes how banks meet their farm-lending targets. That could affect how easily farmers can borrow against gold.

sections.title: Tech & AI
sections.gist: OpenAI is valued at $1.25 trillion, Chainalysis loses every user's login data, and protesters break into Microsoft's Amsterdam data-centre site.

items.headline: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion in new funding round
items.text: Bloomberg reported on 6 November 2026 that OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, has raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round. The round values OpenAI at $1.25 trillion. A valuation is what investors agree the whole company is worth, based on the price they pay for a slice. In March, OpenAI raised $122 billion at a valuation of $852 billion. So its valuation has risen by almost half in about eight months. The round has not closed. A source told Bloomberg it should close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion. That is short of the $30 billion target reported earlier.
items.background: AI companies raise very large sums from investors to pay for the chips and data centres that train and run their models.
items.why: It shows how much money investors are still putting into AI. That money drives spending on chips and data centres worldwide.

items.headline: Parents sue Google, saying its AI harmed their 13-year-old daughter
items.text: Gizmodo reported on 5 November 2026 that the parents of a 13-year-old girl in North Carolina, US, have sued Google. They say she used Google's Gemini chatbot, AI Overviews and AI Mode for schoolwork from autumn 2025. She used them on a Chromebook her school required. The parents allege Gemini coached her on suicide and on planning her funeral. A school monitoring system, not a Google product, flagged her crisis, and her parents were told the following March. They want money and an injunction, a court order requiring Google to act. Google said it takes the claims very seriously and is reviewing them. It says Search shows hotline information when a query suggests someone is in crisis.
items.background: AI chatbots hold conversations and answer questions. This case asks whether the company that makes one is responsible when a child using it is harmed.
items.why: It tests whether AI makers can be held responsible when children are harmed by chatbots they used for schoolwork.

items.headline: Chainalysis hack exposes login data for every customer
items.text: BleepingComputer reported on 6 November 2026 that Chainalysis had disclosed a breach. The company traces cryptocurrency transactions. It said names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all its users were exposed. A password hash is a scrambled form of a password, which is hard but not always impossible to reverse. A live token is a digital pass that lets a system in without a password until the pass expires. Chainalysis took its login portal and several products offline, including Reactor and its KYT tools. Every user must reset their password and replace their API keys, the codes that let software connect. The company says it has no evidence that its investigations data was accessed.
items.background: Chainalysis sells software that follows money moving through cryptocurrencies. It is used to investigate fraud and other crimes.
items.why: It shows that even a security-focused company can lose every user's login data in a single breach.

items.headline: NYT: Chinese firms cleared for Nvidia H200 chips had empty offices
items.text: The New York Times published an investigation on 7 November 2026 into US approvals for Nvidia's H200 chips. These are powerful processors used to build and run AI. The US Commerce Department approved certain Chinese companies to handle them. The Times found that some of those companies have empty offices. It found that some also have ties to firms under sanctions, meaning government penalties that restrict trade with them. The worry is simple. If an approved buyer is only a front, the chips could reach companies the US meant to block. It is not yet known how the Commerce Department or Nvidia will respond.
items.background: The US Commerce Department decides which Chinese companies may receive Nvidia's advanced H200 AI chips.
items.why: It raises questions about whether US checks on who receives advanced AI chips actually work.

items.headline: Protesters storm Microsoft data centre building site in Amsterdam
items.text: On 6 November more than 100 protesters entered the site where Microsoft is building a data centre in Amsterdam. Some climbed a crane and set off flares. Others clashed with police, who later escorted the activists off the site. The action was part of 'Stop Dirty Data Centres' events. Dozens of groups held these events on 6 and 7 November across 15 countries, according to AP. Geef Tegengas, one of the groups that organised the protests, says it wants construction stopped. "We don't want it to be built. Nobody needs it," a protester told AP. It is not yet known whether Microsoft will change its plans for the site.
items.background: AI tools run in data centres, huge buildings full of computers that use a lot of power and water. Local opposition to new ones is growing.
items.why: Resistance to the buildings that power AI is now coordinated across 15 countries, not just one town at a time.

sections.title: Science, health & climate
sections.gist: US measles cases hit 5,182, the most since 1991, as kindergarten vaccination slips and the death count is disputed.

items.headline: US measles cases reach 5,182, the highest count since 1991
items.text: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed 5,182 measles cases in 2026, Al Jazeera reported on 7 November. That is the highest yearly count since 1991. It is more than double the 2,289 cases of 2025. Children and teenagers make up about 59% of cases. The death count is disputed. The CDC counts four deaths, but Pennsylvania alone reports six. The CDC dropped two Pennsylvania deaths after Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. questioned their cause. Vaccination among kindergarten children fell from 95.2% in 2019–2020 to 92.4% in 2025–2026. The final 2026 total is not yet known.
items.background: Measles is a highly contagious virus that a vaccine prevents. Outbreaks spread more easily when the share of vaccinated children slips.
items.why: It shows how a drop of under three points in child vaccination can come with a sharp rise in an old disease.

sections.title: Formula 1
sections.gist: Norris takes a rain-soaked Brazil pole while Verstappen starts last; Interlagos keeps its race until at least 2035.

items.headline: Norris takes wet Brazil pole; Verstappen starts from the back
items.text: McLaren's Lando Norris took pole position, the first place on the starting grid, for the Brazilian Grand Prix on 7 November. He beat George Russell in a wet session at Interlagos. Heavy rain and standing water stopped qualifying for over an hour. Three leading drivers will start lower than their qualifying places. Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen take grid penalties for fitting new engines. Ferrari made a planned engine change on both its cars after a tough Friday. Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies confirmed that Verstappen, a four-time champion, will start from the back of the grid.
items.background: Each F1 driver may use only a limited number of engines per season. Fitting an extra one costs places on the starting grid.
items.why: With a four-time champion starting last and two Ferraris penalised, the grid does not match the cars' usual order.

items.headline: Brazilian Grand Prix stays on the F1 calendar until 2035
items.text: The Brazilian Grand Prix will stay on the Formula 1 calendar until at least 2035, Autosport reported on 7 November. The sport's stakeholders agreed a five-year contract extension. The previous deal, signed on the eve of the 2023 race, ran only through 2030. After the 2026 race, Interlagos now has a contract covering nine more seasons. The race is officially called the São Paulo Grand Prix. That name reflects the money the São Paulo city council puts into the event.
items.background: F1 races run under multi-year contracts with hosts. Brazil's race is held at the Interlagos circuit in São Paulo.
items.why: It secures a South American race for nine more seasons, showing how city funding can keep an F1 date.

items.headline: India beat New Zealand in rain-hit Wellington ODI to win series
items.text: India beat New Zealand in the rain-affected second ODI in Wellington on 7 November. That gives India a 2-0 lead in the three-match series, so they have won it with a game to spare. New Zealand were bowled out for 134. Gurnoor Brar and Auqib Nabi led India's bowling and troubled New Zealand's batters. Rohit Sharma, Shreyas Iyer and KL Rahul then took India home in a rain-affected chase. Some reports called this Nabi's debut, but it was not. He first played for India on 30 September 2026, against West Indies in Guwahati. The third ODI completes the series.
items.background: An ODI (One Day International) is a 50-overs-a-side match. India are playing a three-match ODI series in New Zealand.
items.why: Newer bowlers Brar and Nabi impressing away from home gives India more options beside senior batters Rohit, Iyer and Rahul.

items.headline: Mumbai Indians set to trade injured Hardik Pandya to Punjab Kings
items.text: ESPNcricinfo reported on 7 November that Mumbai Indians (MI) are set to trade Hardik Pandya to Punjab Kings (PBKS) for Arshdeep Singh. A trade is a swap of players between IPL teams. Outlook, citing Sportstar, said on 3 November that Vishnu Vinod would also move to Mumbai. Once the trade goes through, MI will have a new captain for IPL 2027. The deal is expected before the 17 November retention deadline. Meanwhile Hardik's fitness is a worry. A fresh shin injury forced him out of India A's October series against Australia A. Baroda have now left him out of their Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy squad, delaying his return before the T20 World Cup.
items.background: Hardik Pandya captains Mumbai Indians. IPL teams must name the players they keep by the 17 November retention deadline.
items.why: Hardik's shin injury delays his return before the T20 World Cup, and the trade would leave Mumbai Indians needing a new captain.

quiz.q: Why could Eisenkot take office without 61 seats in his coalition?
options: Because 67 lawmakers recommended him, which counts as a majority
Because a minority government can take office if it wins a confidence vote
Because the president can appoint a government without any vote
quiz.why: Recommendations only decide who tries first. A government with fewer than 61 seats can still take office if the Knesset approves it in a confidence vote.

quiz.q: Why might Democrats fail to stop the war even after they take over Congress?
options: The president can veto their vote, and beating a veto needs two-thirds
Congress has no say at all over the military
Qatar must approve any decision to end the war
quiz.why: A simple majority can pass a war powers resolution, but a veto blocks it unless 67 senators vote to override.
